meta.title: Who really said "The only land we ever asked for was enough land to bury our dead"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Colin Powell really said it, word for word — not at Davos, but on an MTV global town hall, 14 February 2002. The State Department transcript confirms it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The only land we ever asked for was enough land to bury our dead'?
meta.ogDescription: Colin Powell said it verbatim on MTV, 14 Feb 2002 — not at Davos in 2003, where he worded it differently. The viral chain-email version is a rewrite.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1937–2021 · U.S. Secretary of State (2001–2005) · Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff (1989–1993)
answer.sourceLine: An unusual result for a name this heavily forged: he really said it, word for word. Powell delivered the sentence on 14 February 2002 during Be Heard, MTV’s globally televised town hall, answering a young woman in the London studio who asked how it felt to represent a country some call the “satan of contemporary politics.” The State Department’s own transcript ↗ carries it verbatim. The version the internet usually cites — a 2003 exchange at Davos with a retired Archbishop of Canterbury — is a different, looser wording of the same idea.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Be Heard: An MTV Global Discussion With Colin Powell”
Secretary of State Colin L. Powell, answering a questioner in the London studio
Washington, D.C., linked by satellite to MTV studios in London, Moscow, New Delhi, Milan, Cairo and São Paulo

source.excerpt: And when all those conflicts were over, what did we do? Did we stay and conquer? Did we say, “Okay, we defeated Germany. Now Germany belongs to us? We defeated Japan, so Japan belongs to us”? No. What did we do? We built them up. We gave them democratic systems which they have embraced totally to their soul. And did we ask for any land? No, the only land we ever asked for was enough land to bury our dead. And that is the kind of nation we are.
trail: The State Department’s archived transcript ↗ of the MTV forum, headed “Secretary Colin L. Powell, Washington, DC, February 14, 2002,” contains the sentence exactly as it is quoted today.

At the World Economic Forum in Davos on 26 January 2003, Powell reached for the same idea in different words, telling George Carey that America has “asked for nothing except enough ground to bury them in” — preserved in the full Davos transcript ↗ and in the State Department’s page of excerpts from the reply to Carey ↗.

Snopes ↗ (24 March 2003) rated the chain-email version True while noting that “the context in which it was delivered has been greatly simplified,” and Truth or Fiction ↗ rates it Mostly Truth, reaching the same conclusion.

The idea predates Powell, though the stone does not: the American Battle Monuments Commission’s list of inscriptions at the Normandy visitor center ↗ credits “all we asked … was enough … soil in which to bury our gallant dead” to Gen. Mark W. Clark, who chaired the commission from 1969 to 1984. That inscription went up when the visitor center was dedicated on 6 June 2007, five years after Powell spoke, and the ABMC page gives no date for when Clark first said the words.
source.excerptNote: The question that prompted it was hostile: a young woman in the London studio — the first overseas questioner of the ninety-minute forum — asked Powell how it felt to represent a country perceived as the “satan of contemporary politics.” He began by rejecting the characterization, then built to “so, far from being the Great Satan, I would say that we are the Great Protector,” and ran through Fascism, Communism, Korea and Vietnam before landing on this line.

author.name: Colin Powell
author.heading: About the speaker
author.metaLine: 1937–2021 · U.S. Army general · Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, 1989–1993 · Secretary of State, 2001–2005
author.bio: Born in Harlem in 1937 to Jamaican immigrant parents, Colin Powell rose through the U.S. Army to four-star general and became the first Black Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, steering the Gulf War before stepping down in 1993. He returned to government as George W. Bush’s Secretary of State, where he was the administration’s most trusted public face — and where his 2003 presentation of Iraq’s alleged weapons of mass destruction to the UN Security Council became, in his own later word, a “blot” on his record. He died in 2021.

misattribution.heading: How it gets garbled
misattribution.intro: The sentence is genuine, but almost every detail attached to it in circulation is wrong. A chain email that spread during the run-up to the Iraq war rewrote the wording, moved the venue, promoted the questioner and invented the question — and quote sites have been copying that version ever since.

items.why: The email quotes Powell as saying “the only amount of land we have ever asked for in return is enough to bury those that did not return.” That polished sentence matches neither transcript. Snopes prints it as the claim ↗, then sets the actual transcript beside it.

Quote sites routinely pin this exact sentence to Powell’s Davos exchange with George Carey. But the Davos transcript ↗ reads “we have asked for nothing except enough ground to bury them in.” The wording quoted here belongs to the MTV forum of 14 February 2002.

The email places the exchange at a conference in England, with the sitting Archbishop asking whether Iraq was “empire building.” In the transcript the questioner introduces himself as “George Carey, the former Archbishop of Canterbury … now happily retired,” the venue is Davos, Switzerland, and his question is about hard power versus soft power — as Truth or Fiction spells out ↗.

Powell was not the first to put it this way. The American Battle Monuments Commission credits the Normandy inscription — “all we asked … was enough … soil in which to bury our gallant dead” — to Gen. Mark W. Clark ↗, the Second World War Italy commander who chaired the commission from 1969 to 1984. Whether Powell knew the line or arrived at it independently is not documented.

misattribution.truthLine: Powell really said it, in exactly these words — on 14 February 2002, on MTV, answering a hostile question from a London studio. The State Department transcript ↗ is the receipt.

context.heading: Why it landed
lead: Five months after 9/11, MTV put the Secretary of State in a Washington studio, wired him to young audiences in six countries and let them ask anything. The first question from the London studio was how it felt to represent a country perceived as the “satan of contemporary politics.” Powell’s reply is a compressed argument about American war aims: we defeated Germany and Japan and did not keep them, we rebuilt them instead, and the only territory we took home was grave plots.

It is a rhetorical move with real history behind it — the same claim is carved into the wall at the Normandy visitor center, credited to Gen. Mark W. Clark. What made Powell’s version travel was the messenger: a four-star general turned diplomat making the case for American restraint to teenagers, live, across six studios of grievance.
detailsBody: Powell reached for the thought again at Davos on 26 January 2003, answering the retired Archbishop of Canterbury George Carey on hard power versus soft power. That reply is longer and less quotable — “we have asked for nothing except enough ground to bury them in” — but it is the exchange that went viral, because a chain email attached a smoothed-up rewrite to it and added a dramatic pin-drop silence that appears in no transcript.

sourcesVerified.claim: The State Department transcript of "Be Heard: An MTV Global Discussion With Colin Powell," headed "Secretary Colin L. Powell, Washington, DC, February 14, 2002," contains verbatim: "And did we ask for any land? No, the only land we ever asked for was enough land to bury our dead. And that is the kind of nation we are," preceded by "Far from being the Great Satan, I would say that we are the Great Protector."

The State Department transcript of Powell's 26 January 2003 Remarks at the World Economic Forum contains George Carey's question (introducing himself as "the former Archbishop of Canterbury... now happily retired") on hard power versus soft power, and Powell's reply "we have asked for nothing except enough ground to bury them in" — a different wording from the MTV version.

The State Department page "Excerpts From Secretary Powell's Response to George Carey" is datelined World Economic Forum, Davos, Switzerland, January 26, 2003, and reproduces both Carey's question and the "enough ground to bury them in" passage.

Snopes (David Mikkelson, published March 24, 2003) rates the chain-email claim True, with the note "The spirit of the quote cited below is true, although the context in which it was delivered has been greatly simplified"; it prints the email's paraphrase ("The only amount of land we have ever asked for in return is enough to bury those that did not return") alongside the actual Davos transcript passage.

Truth or Fiction rates the item Mostly True and states that the widely circulated version wrongly gives the location as England, wrongly identifies the questioner as the sitting Archbishop of Canterbury rather than the former Archbishop George Carey, and mischaracterises the question as being about "empire building" rather than military hard power versus diplomatic soft power.

The ABMC page "About the Inscriptions at the New Normandy Visitors Center" (published June 6, 2007) lists the interior-wall inscription "IF EVER PROOF WERE NEEDED THAT WE FOUGHT FOR A CAUSE AND NOT FOR CONQUEST, IT COULD BE FOUND IN THESE CEMETERIES. HERE WAS OUR ONLY CONQUEST: ALL WE ASKED … WAS ENOUGH … SOIL IN WHICH TO BURY OUR GALLANT DEAD," credited to General Mark W. Clark, Chairman, American Battle Monuments Commission, 1969-1984.

Wikiquote's Colin Powell article places "the only land we ever asked for was enough land to bury our dead. And that is the kind of nation we are" in its sourced 2000s section, citing the MTV Global Discussion of 14 February 2002, and separately records the Davos 26 January 2003 reply to George Carey together with the paraphrase circulated about it.

CNN's contemporaneous report (February 15, 2002) confirms the MTV global forum format — Powell in Washington linked to MTV studios in London, Moscow, New Delhi, Milan, Cairo and Sao Paulo — and that a young woman in London opened the 90-minute session by asking how it felt to represent a country perceived as the "satan of contemporary politics," with Powell answering that America is the "great protector." The article does not itself contain the "bury our dead" sentence.

Wikipedia gives Colin Powell's dates as April 5, 1937 – October 18, 2021, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff October 1, 1989 – September 30, 1993, Secretary of State January 20, 2001 – January 26, 2005, four-star general, born in Harlem to Jamaican immigrant parents.
